text:
B: Hello, Graham. You're Tariq, is it?
A: That's right. Hi.
B: I was looking at your photo earlier, you've got a fair few history books there. What are you reading at the minute?
A: Something on the London docks. How the whole system worked before containerisation. It's quite good, actually.
B: Oh, now you're talking. Industrial stuff's my thing. Canals mostly, the Erewash and the Beeston canal, round here. I was a civil engineer for nearly thirty year, so I'm always looking at the drainage and the lock gates rather than the pretty bits.
A: Civil engineer. What sort of work?
B: Highways and drainage schemes, then project management towards the end, for a consultancy in Derby. Left at fifty-five. Now I'm a postie, part-time, walking round in Chilwell.
A: That's quite a change.
B: It is, yeah. I'll be honest, it was a bad year, stress, and then the heart started doing funny things. So I wanted something with a start and a finish, you know. You go out, you deliver it, you come back, it's done.
A: I get that. My job never finishes. I run operations for a facilities company in London, about forty contracts. Somebody's always got a problem.
B: Oh, I don't miss that. Mind, I still can't help meself. Last month I told me manager how the walks should be split up. Three of them are daft, there's lads crossing each other's routes twice a morning.
A: Did he listen?
B: Did he heck.
A: That's the problem, right. Most people don't want the fix, they just want to not be blamed. I do the scheduling for a few hundred cleaners and security staff, and the hardest part isn't the rota. It's getting the site managers to actually follow it.
B: No, see, I'd put it the other way. If they're not following it, half the time it's because whoever wrote it never walked the job. I was guilty of that meself.
A: Fair point. Partly. Some of them just don't want to.
B: Ha, some of them, yeah. Do you get out of London much?
A: One proper trip a year. Japan last time, Uzbekistan before that. I plan it on a spreadsheet, train times, everything.
B: A spreadsheet! Thank God, I thought it were just me. I did northern Italy last year by rail, every connection on its own tab, backup options in a different colour.
A: Backup options in a different colour. That's the right way to do it.
B: Me daughter thinks I'm mad. I'm learning Italian an' all, four hundred and twelve days on Duolingo.
A: That's commitment. I'm on an app for my written Urdu and I'm nowhere near four hundred days.
B: Get on with it then! You follow football? I'm a Forest man meself.
A: No. Cricket. Pakistan, and Essex.
B: Cricket. Well, at least it's not rugby. I've just had a lady tell me she watches rugby.
A: Pakistan will wind you up more than any football team, I promise you. They collapsed from a winning position last week. Again.
B: Ha, you want to try being Forest. We've had forty years of—
